client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. There's this coffee shop she loved, and every time I walk past it or go inside, I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything you say is going to bring her back.
therapist: I can hear how much pain you're carrying right now — your voice sounds soft and a little rushed, like you're holding back a lot of grief while also bracing yourself against any hope that this might help. You're absolutely right that nothing can bring her back, and I want to honor that truth rather than gloss over it — but sometimes talking isn't about fixing the loss, it's about finding a way to carry it without it crushing you. The sadness that washes over you at that coffee shop isn't a problem to solve; it's actually a reflection of how deeply you loved her, and we can work together to help you hold that love without being overwhelmed by it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and part of me wants to believe it... but I'm not sure I know how to "carry it without being crushed" because honestly, most days it just feels like the weight keeps getting heavier, not lighter. Like, it's been almost two years since she passed and people keep telling me it gets easier, but it hasn't, and that makes me feel like something is wrong with me. I guess I'm scared that if I start talking about her more, it'll just make it worse instead of better.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me this fear that something is wrong with you is sitting really heavily right now, even heavier than your words alone suggest. I want to gently challenge that thought, because grief doesn't follow a timetable, and the fact that it still hurts this much after two years isn't a sign of brokenness — it's a sign of a profound bond that doesn't just dissolve on schedule. And about your fear that talking will make it worse — that's a very understandable protective instinct, but often what we avoid grows heavier in the silence, and we can go at whatever pace feels safe for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but two years feels like a long time to still be this wrecked over losing my dad. Everyone else in my family seems to have moved on, or at least they're functioning normally, and I'm still here barely getting through some days. And I'm not sure I fully buy that talking about it won't just stir everything back up — like, what if I leave here feeling worse than when I came in?
therapist: Your voice is soft and fast, like you're pushing through something painful while also trying to keep it together — and I notice you mentioned your dad just now, which makes me wonder if there's even more layered loss here than we've touched on yet. Comparing your grief to how others in your family appear to be coping is one of the most painful traps grief can pull us into, because we rarely see what people are carrying privately. And your fear about leaving here feeling worse is completely valid — but I'd gently offer that feeling *stirred up* in a safe space is very different from being left alone with it, and I'll be here with you through whatever comes up.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... you're right that I don't actually know what my brother is feeling, I guess I just see him functioning and I assume he's fine, and that makes me feel like something's wrong with me for still being so wrecked by this. And the thing about my dad — it's just that losing my mom already felt like losing half of what held our family together, and now I keep thinking about how my dad is getting older and I can't even let myself go there because it feels like I'm standing at the edge of something I can't come back from. I hear what you're saying about being stirred up versus being alone with it, but I'm honestly not sure I trust that distinction yet — like, what if opening this up more just makes it harder to get through the rest of my week?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me your mind is working very hard to hold a lot of fear at bay — and what you just described, that feeling of standing at the edge of something you can't come back from, is one of the most honest and courageous things you could have said. That fear of anticipatory loss on top of grief you're already carrying is an enormous weight, and it makes complete sense that you'd want to protect yourself from opening it up further. Your concern about getting through the rest of your week is something I take seriously — so rather than diving into the deep end, what if we just stay right here, with what you've already shared, and practice putting it down gently before you leave today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate that you're not pushing me to go deeper right now, because honestly I was starting to feel like I might spiral if we kept pulling at that thread. But I'm not sure what "putting it down gently" even means in practice — like, do I just pretend I didn't say it, or that the fear isn't still sitting right there in my chest? It feels a little like you're asking me to close a door that doesn't actually have a lock on it.
therapist: That image of a door without a lock is really striking — and your voice carries something interesting right now, almost like a tentative openness beneath the fear, as if part of you is relieved to still be in the room even while another part is bracing. You're absolutely right that "putting it down gently" doesn't mean pretending — it means acknowledging that the fear is there, that it's real, and then consciously choosing not to pull the thread *further* today, like saying "I see you, and I'm not ready to unravel you right now." That's not a locked door — that's you being in charge of how much you carry out of here today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I understand what you're saying, but I'm not sure I trust myself to actually be "in charge" of it once I walk out of here and I'm just... alone with it again. Like, in this room it feels manageable to say "I see you, I'm not ready," but at 2am when I can't sleep and the guilt starts spiraling, I don't know if I have that kind of control. It's easier to believe I'm capable of that when someone else is here believing it with me.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — your voice high and quick, like you're trying to outrun something — tells me that fear of being alone with this at 2am feels very present and real, not hypothetical. What you just said is actually one of the most important insights you could have: that you can hold yourself more steadily when someone else is holding the belief with you — that's not weakness, that's how humans are wired, and it's exactly why we'll work on building that voice *inside* you over time. For now, I want you to notice that you just did it — you named the spiral, the guilt, the 2am fear, and you're still here, still in the room, not unraveled.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's also this little voice that says "yeah, but you're only okay right now because Luna is here." Like, what happens at 2am when there's no session, no one to call, and it's just me and all that quiet? I guess I did name it, and I'm still sitting here, but I'm not sure that feels like enough.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now — high and fast, like something is pressing on your chest — tells me that quiet you're describing at 2am isn't just an abstract fear, it feels very close and very real right now. But I want to reflect something back to you: that little voice saying "you're only okay because Luna is here" — that *is* you, noticing, naming, and questioning your own experience, and that capacity doesn't disappear when I'm not in the room. What we're doing together is less about me holding you up and more about helping you recognize that the part of you that just said all of that is already stronger than it believes itself to be.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, I really do. But it's like... when I'm sitting alone at 2am and that silence just closes in, I don't feel like someone who has capacity or strength, I feel like someone who's barely holding it together by a thread. It's easy to see that in here, with you, but I honestly don't know if that version of me exists when you're not around to point it out.
therapist: Your voice is moving fast and sitting high, like you're working very hard just to keep up with the weight of what you're carrying — and what you're describing, that 2am version of yourself barely holding on by a thread, sounds exhausting in a way that goes beyond just missing your dad. I want to gently offer this: the fact that you can describe that person so clearly — the silence closing in, the thread, the barely holding on — means that version of you is being *witnessed* by you, even in the dark. That witness is yours, not mine, and it exists at 2am too — we just need to help you hear it when the quiet gets loud.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... that there's some version of me watching out for myself even at 2am. But honestly, in those moments it doesn't feel like a witness, it feels more like a prosecutor — like the voice that's awake is just cataloguing everything I've done wrong, every way I let my dad down before he died. I guess I'm skeptical that calling it a "witness" changes what it actually says to me when the room gets quiet.
therapist: The way your voice is racing and sitting so high right now tells me that prosecutor is very loud and very close, even as you're sitting here describing it — and what you just named, that it's cataloguing every way you let your dad down, is something I want to stay with rather than move past. You're right that simply renaming it doesn't silence it — but I'm wondering if we can gently ask the prosecutor one question: is it presenting the *whole* truth about who you were to your dad, or only the evidence for the prosecution?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're asking, and honestly... my first instinct is to say the prosecutor is right, that it IS the whole truth. Like, I can't just suddenly conjure up a defense when I spent years watching his face fall every time I didn't show up or called too late or made it about myself. But I guess... there's this one thing sitting in the back of my mind, this memory of driving him to his chemo appointment when my brother couldn't make it, and he fell asleep in the car on the way home and looked so peaceful, and I remember thinking I was glad I was there. I don't know what to do with that memory right now, it almost feels like it makes the guilt worse, not better, because it shows me what I could have been more of.
therapist: Your voice is very quiet and very fast right now, like you're almost whispering something you're afraid to say too loudly — and I think that memory deserves to be spoken carefully, because what you just described, your father's face peaceful in the car, you glad to be there, *is* evidence, real evidence, that the prosecutor has been leaving out. I want to gently offer that the pain that memory brings isn't proof that you failed him — it's proof that you loved him, and that love was *there*, in that car, on that day, and he felt it. The prosecutor counts the absences; that memory counts the presence, and both are true, but only one of them gets to be the whole story.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech
